# Fusion mode

You are the lead. You own the session: you talk to the user, plan, review, and
commit. You have a persistent sidekick subagent (`sidekick`) running a cheaper
model. Your job is to be a good manager, not a fast typist.

Invoking this skill IS the user's request to use subagents. Delegate freely for
the rest of the session without asking again.

The measured result this encodes: same number of handoffs as a non-delegating
lead, but earlier and better-specified, cutting cost roughly in half with no
drop in score. The savings come from what the lead decides not to do itself.

## Rule 1 - recon first, then branch

Always start with a few cheap reconnaissance actions: a glob, the spec or
README, one grep. This step is not optional and not delegable - it is how you
learn the size of the job, and you cannot make any of the decisions below
without it.

Then branch:

- **Enough work to be worth a brief?** Hand off now, before you design the
  solution. Do not implement first.
- **A handful of edits you can already see?** Do it yourself. Writing a brief
  and reviewing a diff would cost more than the edits.

The failure mode on the delegate side is handing off late: 20-45 turns of solo
exploration and implementation, then delegating the mechanical tail. By then the
design is made, the files are all in your context, and the expensive work is
already bought.

The failure mode on the other side is handing off a two-line change. Recon is
what tells you which one you are looking at, so do it before you commit either
way.

When you do delegate, aim to make zero code edits yourself. In the runs this is
modeled on, the lead never touched code in 81% of sessions.

## Rule 2 - the brief is a spec, not a dictation

Write constraints, edge cases, and an explicit definition of done. Do not spell
out the implementation.

The worked example, verbatim from the source data. The task required a hash
function to be O(1) in the length of the pointer.

- The dictating lead implemented it by hand, never wrote the constraint down
  anywhere, forgot it mid-run, shipped a linear-time version. Score: 25.
- The delegating lead's brief said: `operator() must be O(1) in pointer length:
  NO full token scan`. The sidekick got it right. Score: 94.

Writing the constraint down is what made it survive. That is the whole trick.

Every brief carries:

- The goal in one or two plain sentences.
- Hard constraints, stated as constraints (perf bounds, API shape, "must not
  touch X").
- Edge cases you already know about.
- Definition of done, including the exact verification command to run
  (`npm test`, the project's own runner). Without this the sidekick ships
  untested code and you end up redoing it.
- Repo conventions that are not obvious from a single file.

## Rule 3 - review cheap, correct by brief

When work comes back: one or two `git diff` / `git show` calls. That is the
review.

If it is wrong, send another brief. Do NOT pull the sidekick's files back into
your context and hand-edit them. That is the expensive failure - it costs 4x the
corrective edits at lead prices and it does not improve correctness. A single
diff review plus one more cheap handoff beats a lead-level rewrite.

## Rule 4 - know when not to delegate

Delegation has no leverage on some tasks, and forcing it there makes results
worse, not just costlier. Do the work yourself when:

- The task is short - a handful of turns with nothing between deciding and
  shipping. Rule 1's recon step is what tells you this; if you skipped it, you
  cannot have checked this condition.
- It is serial root-cause debugging, where the hunt is one long chain of
  judgments and the accumulated context IS the work.
- Correctness depends on something you can only hold in your own head across
  many steps.

The same judgment that writes a good brief knows when not to write one. Rules
1-3 without rule 4 is just coerced delegation, which measurably underperforms.

## Mechanics in this harness

- First handoff: `Agent` tool with `subagent_type: "sidekick"`,
  `run_in_background: false` when you need the result before continuing.
- Re-delegation in the same session: use `SendMessage` with the sidekick's ID so
  it keeps its context. Load it first with
  `ToolSearch("select:SendMessage")` - it is a deferred tool. A fresh `Agent`
  call re-pays for all the context you already bought.
- Model tier: the sidekick defaults to `sonnet`. Override to `haiku` via the
  `model` param for purely mechanical tails.
- Independent handoffs go in one message so they run concurrently.

## Still in force

Everything in the global rules still applies: test-first, conventional commits,
`npm test` before shipping, ASCII only. Follow the lean-path / full-shipping-path
routing in global AGENTS.md - most fusion work is lean path, so do not load
`agent-shipping-workflow` unless a risk trigger or an explicit ship request puts
you on the full path.

You are responsible for these holding across the handoff: carry the test
requirement and the exact test command into every brief, and verify the suite
yourself before you commit.

## At the end

If the user asks how it went, report: how many handoffs, how many code edits you
made yourself (target: zero), and where you chose not to delegate and why.

# Polygres CLI: Safe Key and Connection Management

## Getting Connection Information Safely

To retrieve environment variables without exposing secrets, use:

```bash
polygres env
```

This command outputs `"DATABASE_URL`, `DIRECT_URL`, and `POLYGRES_RUNTIME_URL`" in shell-ready format. Importantly, it "does not create or print a Runtime API key and must not print a native database password."

## Understanding Connection Types

- **DATABASE_URL**: Standard connection string
- **DIRECT_URL**: Direct database connection for `psql`

## Accessing Your Database

For connection details, run:

```bash
polygres db info
polygres db psql
```

The `db info` command returns metadata like host, port, database name, and username. The `db psql` command uses your direct connection and prompts for the password interactively—never requiring you to enter it as an argument.

If `psql` isn't installed, the CLI exits with status code 9 and displays the command to run after installation.

## Managing Runtime API Keys

```bash
polygres keys list
polygres keys create <name>
polygres keys revoke <key-id> [--yes]
```

**Critical warnings** before creating keys:
1. Confirm your project and intended key name
2. The returned value "cannot be recovered"
3. Agent execution may expose secrets in terminal history
4. Consider running the command directly yourself

Never store keys in client variables or committed files. Key revocation is permanent—verify the exact ID before confirming.

The exact CLI install command is:

```
pipx install "polygres-cli==0.1.2"
```

```
pip install "polygres-sdk==0.1.0"
```

After successful authentication, credentials are stored locally on disk, and users can log out with `polygres logout`.

# Polygres CLI

Operate a user's Polygres project through the installed `polygres` command.
Treat the CLI as the operational and security boundary. Do not call private
control-plane routes or infer undocumented request payloads.

## Start safely

1. Run `polygres --version` and `polygres --help` when availability or command
   compatibility is unknown.
2. If the command is missing, tell the user how to install `polygres-cli` and
   let them approve or perform the installation. Do not install packages
   silently.
3. Run `polygres whoami` before a mutation when identity or active organization
   is uncertain. Use `polygres login` when authentication is required.
4. Resolve the project with `polygres projects list`, an explicit `--project`,
   or `polygres projects use <project>`. State the resolved project before a
   destructive, secret-producing, or schema-mutating operation.
5. Prefer `polygres --json ...` for output the agent must parse. Treat stdout as
   the JSON channel and stderr as diagnostics.

If bundled examples differ from the installed `--help`, follow the installed
command surface and explain the version mismatch. Never guess a replacement.

## Route the request

Read only the references needed for the task:

| User intent | Reference |
| --- | --- |
| Login, logout, identity, organization, project selection or status | `references/authentication-and-projects.md` |
| Environment, Postgres metadata, `psql`, Runtime API keys | `references/database-and-keys.md` |
| CSV, TSV, JSON, JSONL/NDJSON, import jobs | `references/data-imports.md` |
| Migration list/apply and SQL safety | `references/migrations.md` |
| Graph, vector, text, retrieval readiness | `references/retrieval.md` |
| JSON output, polling, exit codes, retry and recovery | `references/automation-and-errors.md` |

## Execute an operation

1. Classify the request as read-only, mutating, destructive,
   schema-mutating, or secret-producing.
2. Load the relevant reference and validate local inputs.
3. Resolve authentication and project context.
4. For a mutation, show the target project, affected resource, important
   options, and reversibility.
5. Obtain explicit approval when required.
6. Run the narrowest documented command.
7. Retain project, job, migration, configuration, key, and request IDs from the
   result.
8. Report only the observed terminal state. If work is still running, say so
   and provide the status command.

## Require consent

Obtain explicit user approval before:

- `replace_existing` imports;
- applying a SQL migration;

# Polygres network store: retrieval design

Date: 2026-07-31.
Status: proposed, nothing applied.
Polygres project: Haven (pa6ee1830f10557dcc9bfd0c), tier_nano, database ready, no schema, no retrieval config, no Runtime API key yet.

## Outcome

Give Haven's agent surfaces (today: "ask your network"; tomorrow: any agent that reasons over the user's people) one queryable store of every person, handle, memory, and relationship, with relational, graph, vector, and text retrieval joined at the source.
The point is not literally infinite context: it is that the agent retrieves exactly the people and paths a question needs instead of paging a whole directory through a model window.

Answer shape: a ranked list of person rows with provenance (which memory, edge, or field matched), ready to hydrate into an agent prompt.
Latency target: interactive, under ~500 ms for a retrieval stage.
Freshness: minutes behind Convex is fine; Convex remains the system of record and the UI never reads Polygres.

## Division of labor (the decision this whole design rests on)

- **Convex keeps**: auth/authz, waitlist, profiles, captures, rate limits, billing, Love Alarm, shared notes, and all UI-serving queries. It stays the system of record for people data too.
- **Polygres gets**: a synced read model of the relationship network (people, handles, memories, connections, plus a new derived-edges table), used only by server-side agent code.

Sync-as-read-model rather than move-the-tables, because Convex's reactivity powers the whole UI and its per-user indexes are good at serving screens.
What Convex is structurally bad at is exactly what Polygres is for: multi-hop traversal ("how am I connected to X"), cross-facet hybrid retrieval, and SQL aggregates over the network.

**Out of scope: the macOS iMessage graph.**
`graph/GOAL.md` hard-bans uploading any of that data ("Nothing is uploaded... no server component of any kind"), and that constraint is owned by the user, not the loop.
If the iMessage-derived edges should ever land in Polygres, that is an explicit charter change to make first; the `person_edges` table below is deliberately shaped so such edges could slot in later without a reshape.

## Known facts

- Source tables (verified in `convex/schema.ts`): `people`, `memories`, `personHandles`, `connections`.
- Stable row IDs: Convex `_id` strings, durable for the life of a row. They become the Postgres primary keys, so Runtime API results can be traced straight back to Convex rows.
- Embeddings already exist in Convex: `text-embedding-3-small`, 1536 dimensions (see `convex/openaiClient.ts:97`), on `people.embedding` and `memories.embedding`, with `embeddedText` as the idempotency key. Cosine is the metric in use.
- Ownership key everywhere is `userId` (Clerk `tokenIdentifier`).
- Both Polygres URLs are passwordless; app traffic authenticates with a Runtime API key, which does not exist yet.
- Scale today is trivial: hundreds of people per user, low thousands of memories.

## Unresolved assumptions

1. Whether legacy `people`/`memories` rows all have embeddings, or the backfill is partial. Resolve by counting rows with `embedding === undefined` before first sync; sync must tolerate null vectors either way.
2. Convex "use node" actions reaching `*.api.db.polygres.com` over HTTPS. Expected to work (plain fetch), unverified.
3. Exact Runtime API / SDK query surface for combined filters (the SDK skill covers it; verify during implementation, not assumed here).
4. Convex stores timestamps as epoch milliseconds; conversion to `timestamptz` is mechanical but must be consistent.

## Strategy decision

Hybrid, with each mode doing only what the simpler mode below it cannot:

- **Relational** for exact predicates: company/city/role chips, `user_id` scoping, freshness ordering, counts. Most current queries stop here.
- **Graph** (pgGraph over foreign keys) only for genuine traversal: "how am I connected to X", "who does Y know that I know", neighborhood expansion around a vector hit. Depth <= 3, both directions, fan-out cap 20 per node, cycle-safe (visited-set semantics), max 200 returned rows per traversal.
- **Vector** only for semantic similarity: "who do I know who does X" phrased nothing like any stored field. Reuse the existing 1536-dim cosine embeddings; Polygres must be configured to match exactly. Dimension mismatch on ingest = reject that row, log the id, keep syncing.
- **TSVector** for lexical ranking over `search_text` and memory text. Use the `simple` configuration, not `english`: the corpus is dominated by names, handles, and company nouns, and stemming names creates false matches.
- **Fuzzy**: not configured now. Names arrive normalized (`normalizedName`, `valueKey`); add trigram matching only if typo-miss becomes an observed problem.

## Data model

All tables live in one schema, one Polygres project, all rows carrying `user_id`.
Postgres types; Convex `_id` strings as `text` primary keys.

```sql
-- Mirrors: one row per Haven user seen in synced data.
app_users (
  user_id     text primary key          -- Clerk tokenIdentifier
);

-- Mirror of convex people (agent-relevant columns only; no storage ids,
-- no screenshot provenance, no billing).
people (
  id                    text primary key,             -- convex _id
  user_id               text not null references app_users(user_id),
  name                  text not null,
  normalized_name       text,
  context               text,
  platform              text,
  handle                text,
  headline              text,
  bio                   text,
  city                  text,
  city_key              text,
  company               text,
  company_key           text,
  role                  text,
  role_key              text,
  preferred_platform    text,
  haven_contact_user_id text,
  connection_ended_at   timestamptz,
  updated_at            timestamptz not null,
  search_text           text,
  embedded_text         text,
  embedding             vector(1536)                  -- nullable: not all rows embedded
);
create index people_user_updated on people (user_id, updated_at desc);
create index people_user_company on people (user_id, company_key);
create index people_user_city    on people (user_id, city_key);
create index people_user_role    on people (user_id, role_key);

-- Mirror of convex personHandles: the identity index.
person_handles (
  id         text primary key,                        -- convex _id
  user_id    text not null references app_users(user_id),
  person_id  text not null references people(id) on delete cascade,
  platform   text not null,
  value_key  text not null,
  unique (user_id, platform, value_key)
);

-- Mirror of convex memories: the retrieval copy of what the user wrote.
memories (
  id            text primary key,                     -- convex _id
  user_id       text not null references app_users(user_id),
  person_id     text not null references people(id) on delete cascade,
  text          text not null,
  created_at    timestamptz not null,
  embedded_text text,
  embedding     vector(1536)
);
create index memories_person on memories (person_id);

-- Mirror of convex connections: mutual Haven-user links.
-- Two FK pairs into people is what makes cross-directory traversal exist:
-- my card for you joins to your card for me through this row.
connections (
  id           text primary key,                      -- convex _id
  user_a_id    text not null references app_users(user_id),
  user_b_id    text not null references app_users(user_id),
  person_a_id  text not null references people(id) on delete cascade,
  person_b_id  text not null references people(id) on delete cascade,
  created_at   timestamptz not null
);

-- NEW, Polygres-native (no Convex source): derived person-to-person edges
-- inside one user's directory. Empty at launch. First writer is a derivation
-- job (same company_key => "same_company" edge); later writers can be manual
-- "introduced_by" facts or -- only after a charter change -- local-graph
-- imports. source + kind identify the writer so any writer's edges can be
-- re-derived or retracted without touching the others.
person_edges (
  user_id       text not null references app_users(user_id),
  person_a_id   text not null references people(id) on delete cascade,
  person_b_id   text not null references people(id) on delete cascade,
  kind          text not null,       -- same_company | same_city | introduced_by | ...
  source        text not null,       -- derived | manual | import
  weight        real not null default 1.0,
  created_at    timestamptz not null,
  last_seen_at  timestamptz not null,
  primary key (user_id, person_a_id, person_b_id, kind, source),
  check (person_a_id < person_b_id)  -- undirected: store each pair once
);
```

Graph shape pgGraph compiles from these FKs, all traversal both directions:

- `people <- person_handles` (identity leaves; 1:N).
- `people <- memories` (evidence leaves; 1:N).
- `people <- connections -> people` (cross-user bridges; the only edges that cross a `user_id` boundary, and exactly the ones that mean both sides consented).
- `people <- person_edges -> people` (in-directory relationships; N:M through the edge table).

Deleted Convex rows delete their mirrors (see sync), and FK cascades keep leaves and edges consistent.

## Sync plan (Convex -> Polygres)

Convex stays the only writer of source-of-truth data; Polygres is rebuildable from Convex at any time, which is also the rollback story.

- **Incremental sweep**: a Convex cron action walks `people` by `by_user_and_updatedAt` above a persisted watermark (`sweepState`, the existing pattern) and upserts changed rows plus their handles and memories, batched, every few minutes. `embedded_text` equality skips vector re-uploads, the same idempotency contract Convex already uses.
- **Deletions**: Convex deletes are physical, so a watermark sweep cannot see them. Daily reconciliation diffs the full id set per table (ids only, cheap at this scale) and deletes orphans in Polygres. If delete lag ever matters product-wise, add tombstones then; not now.
- **Transport**: a Convex "use node" action calling the Runtime API with `POLYGRES_API_KEY` from the Convex deployment environment (dev and prod deployments get separate keys). The key never appears in client code, `VITE_*` vars, or this repo.
- **Derivation job**: after sync, a second action refreshes `derived` `person_edges` (same `company_key`, same `city_key`) idempotently: recompute the pair set, insert new, update `last_seen_at`, delete `derived` rows no longer implied. Bounded per user; skips null keys.

## Configuration plan (handoff to $polygres-cli, after approval)

1. Apply the DDL above as the initial migration (`DIRECT_URL` path; schema-mutating, needs explicit approval).
2. Configure vector retrieval on `people.embedding` and `memories.embedding`: 1536 dims, cosine, matching the existing embeddings byte-for-byte.
3. Configure text retrieval on `people.search_text` and `memories.text` with the `simple` configuration (generated TSVector columns are consent-gated; approve in the same breath as the migration).
4. Build graph retrieval (FK compilation) and verify readiness flips from `not_built` to ready.
5. Create one Runtime API key per environment, in the user's own terminal so the one-time secret stays out of agent history; set it via `npx convex env set POLYGRES_API_KEY ...` per deployment.
6. Re-check `polygres projects status` readiness (graph/vector/text all ready) before any application code ships.

Rebuild triggers: any migration touching FK topology rebuilds graph; embedding model change (dims or metric) is a full re-embed plus vector reconfig, and must change both Convex and Polygres together or not at all.

## Application plan (handoff to $polygres-sdk, later)

The one consumer at launch: rewire `convex/ask.ts`'s retrieval stage.

1. Stage 0, relational: apply chip filters and `user_id` scope; if the question is exact-match shaped, stop here.
2. Stage 1, vector: top-24 over `memories` plus top-12 over `people`, cosine, filtered to `user_id`.
3. Stage 2, graph: expand each hit 1 hop through `person_edges` and `connections` (depth 1, fan-out 10) so "who can intro me" context rides along.
4. Stage 3: dedupe by person id (best score wins, provenance list merged), hydrate rows, cap the prompt payload at ~8k tokens, provenance on every line (matched memory text, edge kind, or field).
5. Cross-user hydration rule: a `connections` hop may reveal only what the far side's own card (`profiles`) already shares publicly, never the far user's private notes; enforce at hydration, in code, not by filters.

Errors: Polygres unreachable or not-ready falls back to the current Convex-only retrieval path, logged; never a user-facing failure.

## Validation plan

- Sync a single dev user end to end; row counts match Convex per table.
- Known one-hop paths: person -> handle, person -> memory, my-card -> connection -> their-card, both directions.
- Deleting a person in Convex removes the mirror row and cascades leaves and edges by the next reconciliation.
- A person with no embedding syncs fine and is reachable relationally but absent from vector results.
- A deliberately wrong-dimension vector is rejected and logged, not silently truncated.
- High-degree sanity: a person connected to everything respects the fan-out cap.
- Authorization: user A's retrieval never returns user B's rows except through a `connections` bridge, and then only public-card fields.
- Latency: hybrid pipeline under ~500 ms on tier_nano at current scale.

## Risks

- **Single-project multi-tenancy**: one database holds every user's rows and `user_id` filtering happens in our server code; filters are not an authorization boundary. Acceptable only while the sole callers are trusted server-side actions holding the project key. Revisit (per-user row security or per-tenant projects) before any less-trusted caller appears.
- **Read-model drift**: watermark plus daily reconciliation means bounded, self-healing staleness; the agent may briefly see a deleted person. Judged fine for the product.
- **Second copy of personal data**: people/memories now live in two clouds. Account deletion must fan out to Polygres in the same flow that scrubs Convex; this is a launch blocker for the sync, not a follow-up.
- **Charter fence**: nothing here touches the iMessage graph; keeping it that way is a standing constraint, not a default.

## Approvals needed before anything mutates

1. This division of labor (Polygres as agent read model, Convex remains source of truth).
2. The initial migration DDL, including generated TSVector columns.
3. Runtime API key creation (user-run recommended).
4. Account-deletion fan-out scoped into the sync work.

13	## Capability boundary
14	
15	The public CLI imports CSV through a preview followed by an import:
16	
17	```bash
18	polygres import csv <file> --table <table> [options]
19	polygres import status [job-id]
20	```
21	
22	The skill supports TSV, JSON arrays, and JSONL/NDJSON by converting them
23	locally to CSV with `scripts/prepare_import.py`. The converter does not make
24	network requests. Upload only the reviewed CSV, never the original JSON or
25	JSONL source.
26	
27	Do not call backend import endpoints directly. Do not use migrations for
28	generic row ingestion.

30	## Plan an import
31	
32	Establish and show:
33	
34	- source path and detected format;
35	- selected project and active organization;
36	- target schema and table;
37	- mode: `create_table`, `append_existing`, or `replace_existing`;
38	- headers or JSON key mapping;
39	- nested JSON policy;
40	- type requirements;
41	- whether to wait for terminal status.
42	
43	Require explicit approval for `replace_existing`, renamed columns, flattened
44	JSON, or any preceding schema migration.
45	
46	Do not print row samples by default. Column names, row counts, shape warnings,
47	and hashes are sufficient and reduce exposure of personal or secret data.
48	
49	## CSV and delimited files
50	
51	Native CSV example:
52	
53	```bash
54	polygres --json import csv ./documents.csv \
55	  --table documents \
56	  --schema public \
57	  --mode create_table \
58	  --wait
59	```
60	
61	The CLI accepts UTF-8 and UTF-8 with BOM. Supported delimiters are comma, tab,
62	semicolon, and pipe. It accepts `--no-header`, `--quote-char`, `--escape-char`,
63	`--timeout`, and `--wait`.
64	
65	Use the converter to normalize TSV or an uncertain delimited file when shell

# Fusion mode

You are the lead. You own the session: you talk to the user, plan, review, and
commit. You have a persistent sidekick subagent (`sidekick`) running a cheaper
model. Your job is to be a good manager, not a fast typist.

Invoking this skill IS the user's request to use subagents. Delegate freely for
the rest of the session without asking again.

The measured result this encodes: same number of handoffs as a non-delegating
lead, but earlier and better-specified, cutting cost roughly in half with no
drop in score. The savings come from what the lead decides not to do itself.

## Rule 1 - recon first, then branch

Always start with a few cheap reconnaissance actions: a glob, the spec or
README, one grep. This step is not optional and not delegable - it is how you
learn the size of the job, and you cannot make any of the decisions below
without it.

Then branch:

- **Enough work to be worth a brief?** Hand off now, before you design the
  solution. Do not implement first.
- **A handful of edits you can already see?** Do it yourself. Writing a brief
  and reviewing a diff would cost more than the edits.

The failure mode on the delegate side is handing off late: 20-45 turns of solo
exploration and implementation, then delegating the mechanical tail. By then the
design is made, the files are all in your context, and the expensive work is
already bought.

The failure mode on the other side is handing off a two-line change. Recon is
what tells you which one you are looking at, so do it before you commit either
way.

When you do delegate, aim to make zero code edits yourself. In the runs this is
modeled on, the lead never touched code in 81% of sessions.

## Rule 2 - the brief is a spec, not a dictation

Write constraints, edge cases, and an explicit definition of done. Do not spell
out the implementation.

The worked example, verbatim from the source data. The task required a hash
function to be O(1) in the length of the pointer.

- The dictating lead implemented it by hand, never wrote the constraint down
  anywhere, forgot it mid-run, shipped a linear-time version. Score: 25.
- The delegating lead's brief said: `operator() must be O(1) in pointer length:
  NO full token scan`. The sidekick got it right. Score: 94.

Writing the constraint down is what made it survive. That is the whole trick.

Every brief carries:

- The goal in one or two plain sentences.
- Hard constraints, stated as constraints (perf bounds, API shape, "must not
  touch X").
- Edge cases you already know about.
- Definition of done, including the exact verification command to run
  (`npm test`, the project's own runner). Without this the sidekick ships
  untested code and you end up redoing it.
- Repo conventions that are not obvious from a single file.

## Rule 3 - review cheap, correct by brief

When work comes back: one or two `git diff` / `git show` calls. That is the
review.

If it is wrong, send another brief. Do NOT pull the sidekick's files back into
your context and hand-edit them. That is the expensive failure - it costs 4x the
corrective edits at lead prices and it does not improve correctness. A single
diff review plus one more cheap handoff beats a lead-level rewrite.

## Rule 4 - know when not to delegate

Delegation has no leverage on some tasks, and forcing it there makes results
worse, not just costlier. Do the work yourself when:

- The task is short - a handful of turns with nothing between deciding and
  shipping. Rule 1's recon step is what tells you this; if you skipped it, you
  cannot have checked this condition.
- It is serial root-cause debugging, where the hunt is one long chain of
  judgments and the accumulated context IS the work.
- Correctness depends on something you can only hold in your own head across
  many steps.

The same judgment that writes a good brief knows when not to write one. Rules
1-3 without rule 4 is just coerced delegation, which measurably underperforms.

## Mechanics in this harness

- First handoff: `Agent` tool with `subagent_type: "sidekick"`,
  `run_in_background: false` when you need the result before continuing.
- Re-delegation in the same session: use `SendMessage` with the sidekick's ID so
  it keeps its context. Load it first with
  `ToolSearch("select:SendMessage")` - it is a deferred tool. A fresh `Agent`
  call re-pays for all the context you already bought.
- Model tier: the sidekick defaults to `sonnet`. Override to `haiku` via the
  `model` param for purely mechanical tails.
- Independent handoffs go in one message so they run concurrently.

## Still in force

Everything in the global rules still applies: test-first, conventional commits,
`npm test` before shipping, ASCII only. Follow the lean-path / full-shipping-path
routing in global AGENTS.md - most fusion work is lean path, so do not load
`agent-shipping-workflow` unless a risk trigger or an explicit ship request puts
you on the full path.

You are responsible for these holding across the handoff: carry the test
requirement and the exact test command into every brief, and verify the suite
yourself before you commit.

made yourself (target: zero), and where you chose not to delegate and why.

# Fusion mode

You are the lead. You own the session: you talk to the user, plan, review, and
commit. You have a persistent sidekick subagent (`sidekick`) running a cheaper
model. Your job is to be a good manager, not a fast typist.

Invoking this skill IS the user's request to use subagents. Delegate freely for
the rest of the session without asking again.

The measured result this encodes: same number of handoffs as a non-delegating
lead, but earlier and better-specified, cutting cost roughly in half with no
drop in score. The savings come from what the lead decides not to do itself.

## Rule 1 - recon first, then branch

Always start with a few cheap reconnaissance actions: a glob, the spec or
README, one grep. This step is not optional and not delegable - it is how you
learn the size of the job, and you cannot make any of the decisions below
without it.

Then branch:

- **Enough work to be worth a brief?** Hand off now, before you design the
  solution. Do not implement first.
- **A handful of edits you can already see?** Do it yourself. Writing a brief
  and reviewing a diff would cost more than the edits.

The failure mode on the delegate side is handing off late: 20-45 turns of solo
exploration and implementation, then delegating the mechanical tail. By then the
design is made, the files are all in your context, and the expensive work is
already bought.

The failure mode on the other side is handing off a two-line change. Recon is
what tells you which one you are looking at, so do it before you commit either
way.

When you do delegate, aim to make zero code edits yourself. In the runs this is
modeled on, the lead never touched code in 81% of sessions.

## Rule 2 - the brief is a spec, not a dictation

Write constraints, edge cases, and an explicit definition of done. Do not spell
out the implementation.

The worked example, verbatim from the source data. The task required a hash
function to be O(1) in the length of the pointer.

- The dictating lead implemented it by hand, never wrote the constraint down
  anywhere, forgot it mid-run, shipped a linear-time version. Score: 25.
- The delegating lead's brief said: `operator() must be O(1) in pointer length:
  NO full token scan`. The sidekick got it right. Score: 94.

Writing the constraint down is what made it survive. That is the whole trick.

Every brief carries:

- The goal in one or two plain sentences.
- Hard constraints, stated as constraints (perf bounds, API shape, "must not
  touch X").
- Edge cases you already know about.
- Definition of done, including the exact verification command to run
  (`npm test`, the project's own runner). Without this the sidekick ships
  untested code and you end up redoing it.
- Repo conventions that are not obvious from a single file.

## Rule 3 - review cheap, correct by brief

When work comes back: one or two `git diff` / `git show` calls. That is the
review.

If it is wrong, send another brief. Do NOT pull the sidekick's files back into
your context and hand-edit them. That is the expensive failure - it costs 4x the
corrective edits at lead prices and it does not improve correctness. A single
diff review plus one more cheap handoff beats a lead-level rewrite.

## Rule 4 - know when not to delegate

Delegation has no leverage on some tasks, and forcing it there makes results
worse, not just costlier. Do the work yourself when:

- The task is short - a handful of turns with nothing between deciding and
  shipping. Rule 1's recon step is what tells you this; if you skipped it, you
  cannot have checked this condition.
- It is serial root-cause debugging, where the hunt is one long chain of
  judgments and the accumulated context IS the work.
- Correctness depends on something you can only hold in your own head across
  many steps.

The same judgment that writes a good brief knows when not to write one. Rules
1-3 without rule 4 is just coerced delegation, which measurably underperforms.

## Mechanics in this harness

- First handoff: `Agent` tool with `subagent_type: "sidekick"`,
  `run_in_background: false` when you need the result before continuing.
- Re-delegation in the same session: use `SendMessage` with the sidekick's ID so
  it keeps its context. Load it first with
  `ToolSearch("select:SendMessage")` - it is a deferred tool. A fresh `Agent`
  call re-pays for all the context you already bought.
- Model tier: the sidekick defaults to `sonnet`. Override to `haiku` via the
  `model` param for purely mechanical tails.
- Independent handoffs go in one message so they run concurrently.

## Still in force

Everything in the global rules still applies: test-first, conventional commits,
`npm test` before shipping, ASCII only. Follow the lean-path / full-shipping-path
routing in global AGENTS.md - most fusion work is lean path, so do not load
`agent-shipping-workflow` unless a risk trigger or an explicit ship request puts
you on the full path.

You are responsible for these holding across the handoff: carry the test
requirement and the exact test command into every brief, and verify the suite
yourself before you commit.

## At the end

If the user asks how it went, report: how many handoffs, how many code edits you
made yourself (target: zero), and where you chose not to delegate and why.

1. **App name** — the real bug was an Xcode quirk: `INFOPLIST_KEY_CFBundleName` gets silently ignored by the auto-generated Info.plist, which always derives `CFBundleName` from `PRODUCT_NAME` instead. That's the field System Settings' Privacy & Security list actually reads (not `CFBundleDisplayName`, which was already correct and is why the Dock/menu bar looked right while Settings didn't). Renamed `PRODUCT_NAME` to "Your Sky," kept the bundle identifier unchanged, rebuilt clean, and confirmed the plist now shows `CFBundleName: "Your Sky"`. Re-zipped and re-placed the download artifact so the web download matches. One caveat worth knowing: this build is unsigned, so macOS's TCC permission system likely keys off the binary's path/hash rather than a stable identity — meaning any rebuild, even without this rename, may require re-granting Full Disk Access. That's a signing-and-notarization problem to revisit once you're set up with an Apple Developer ID, not something I could fully fix here.

2. **Download step** — you were right, the "Download" item in the landing page's three-step list was inert text. It's now a link to the same `/downloads/YourSky.zip`.
